name: Datalog
title: Datalog (Soufflé 2.4)

type.text: **Predicates are dynamically typed**: A term's type is its arity and position, known only at evaluation time, so an arity mismatch appears when the rule runs
**No sum types**: An alternative is a separate predicate or a tagged term, and nothing checks that the cases are exhaustive
**No generics**: Every rule is polymorphic over any ground term by construction, so there is no declared type parameter
**Predicates live in one flat name space**: Two programs that define the same predicate name can collide unless the engine provides a module system
**There is no module boundary**: Basic Datalog exposes every predicate to every query; module or component systems are implementation-specific
**A rule's effects are not tracked**: A rule derives facts, but the program has no construct that states whether a predicate is read-only or mutating
**User-defined functors cross into native code unchecked**: A functor declared by signature is implemented in the host language, and the engine does not verify it
**Unification and recursion are the core mechanisms**: A few rules express transitive closure and fixed-point computation without loops

construction.text: **Facts and rules share one form**: A fact is a rule with an empty body, so the program is a set of logical statements
**Rules compose without mutable state**: The result of one rule is used by another through shared predicates, not through assignment
**Negation requires stratification**: A program with unstratified negation has no clear semantics, so the engine rejects it or applies a fixed stratification policy

memory.text: **Memory reclamation is the engine's decision**: Derived facts and indices are released when the engine chooses, not when a rule finishes
**A rule never names an address or allocates explicitly**: The engine materialises relations and indices without manual memory management
**Large intermediate relations can exhaust memory**: A recursive rule that generates many tuples can exceed the engine's working set

error.text: **Syntax errors are caught at parse time**: Rule heads, bodies, and literals are checked for well-formedness before evaluation
**Type and arity errors surface at evaluation**: A predicate used with the wrong arity fails only when that rule is evaluated

concurrency.text: **Evaluation is naturally set-based and read-only**: A Datalog program derives a fixed point from facts and rules without explicit locking
**Concurrency is not part of the language**: Parallel evaluation, transactions, and isolation are provided by the engine, not by the rules

platform.text: **The rule syntax is portable across systems**: A Datalog program of facts and Horn clauses can move between Soufflé, LogicBlox, and academic engines with small changes
**Extensions differ widely**: Aggregations, negation, arithmetic, and components have different syntax and semantics in each engine
**The language is a poor fit for general-purpose work**: File handling, text processing, and user interfaces belong in another language

performance.text: **Evaluation is interpretation or compilation of rules**: A program is evaluated by a rule engine or translated to another target, so tight numeric loops trail a hand-written implementation
**Semi-naive evaluation avoids redundant work**: Recursive rules compute only the newly derived tuples per iteration
**Indices are chosen automatically**: The engine selects B-trees or hash indices for predicates without hand-tuning

ecosystem.text: **There is no standard package manager**: The language ships no distribution mechanism; each engine has its own way to include libraries
**The ecosystem is small and academic**: Libraries, tooling, and practitioners are far fewer than for SQL or mainstream languages
**Several mature engines exist**: Soufflé, LogicBlox, Datomic, Cozo, and XSB cover different points in the performance and expressiveness space

evolution.text: **Standardisation moves slowly**: Datalog has no living standards committee, so new features arrive as engine extensions
**The core rule language is stable**: Facts, rules, and stratified negation have been unchanged for decades

domain.text: **Adopting Datalog means adopting a rule engine**: The language is inseparable from the engine that evaluates the fixed point
**Excellent fit for program analysis and knowledge bases**: Reachability, points-to, and policy rules map directly to recursive rules
**Some domains need extensions beyond pure Datalog**: Arithmetic, aggregation, and updates require engine-specific constructs
**Datalog is used to derive answers from facts and rules**: A query asks whether a predicate holds, and the engine computes the least fixed point

learning.text: **Declarative rule thinking is a different model**: A developer must write what is true rather than how to compute it, and recursion must be understood to read a program
**The core language is tiny**: Facts, rules, and queries are the only constructs beyond built-in predicates
**Negation and aggregation semantics must be learned**: Stratification, choice, and aggregate semantics differ between engines

syntax.text: **Rules read as logical statements**: `ancestor(X, Y) :- parent(X, Y).` is close to its intended meaning
**Comma has several roles**: It separates arguments in a literal, conjoins literals in a body, and separates facts, so context decides the meaning

testing.text: **Type and arity faults surface only at run time**: A wrong predicate name or arity is not rejected until the rule is evaluated
**No monotonic clock is published**: Timing a rule evaluation relies on the engine's wall clock or an external stopwatch
**A query is itself a test**: Asking whether a fact is derivable exercises the rules directly

security.text: **Dynamic typing weakens the trust boundary**: A term from an untrusted source is separated from a rule only by an explicit check
**No pointer arithmetic or buffer access**: The language operates on relations and terms, so memory-safety vulnerabilities cannot be written in Datalog source
**User-defined functors can execute arbitrary native code**: A functor is a hand-written extension that the engine runs with its own privileges

reproducibility.text: **There is no standard build manifest**: Reproducing a result depends on pinning the engine version and the input facts by hand

supplychain.text: **No package registry exists for Datalog modules**: There is therefore no registry namespace to confuse or hijack
**No advisory feed joins engine vulnerabilities to versions**: Known issues are tracked manually per engine

observability.text: **No stable tracing and metrics standard is part of the language**: Observability is provided by the engine and its logs
**No structured logging is defined in the language**: Diagnostics are engine log entries with their own format
**A failed evaluation leaves no standard post-mortem artifact**: The engine may log the error, but the language does not mandate a stack trace

feedback.text: **The edit-test loop is submitting rules to the engine**: There is no separate compile step for small programs
**No fast in-editor analysis is standard**: Type and arity errors are found when the engine evaluates the rules
**No source-level debugger ships with the language**: Debugging is done through logs, provenance, and engine tools

interop.text: **User-defined functors call native code**: Soufflé and other engines let a rule call a function implemented in C or another host language
**A Datalog program runs only inside a rule engine**: There is no portable target outside that context

governance.text: **No single vendor controls Datalog**: Multiple academic and commercial engines coexist
**The core rule syntax is documented in textbooks and papers**: The language surface is not a closed secret
**No conformance suite exists**: Independent engines cannot run a shared test suite against the language semantics
**Parser implementations are available**: Open-source engines publish their parsers, so third-party tools can read Datalog

tradeoffs: **Recursion is the central feature**: Expressive fixed-point queries are concise, but the developer must think in recursive rules
**Dynamic typing keeps rules polymorphic**: A single rule works over any ground term, but arity and type errors move to evaluation
**Stratified negation is a semantics choice**: The language documents the restriction and leaves more flexible negation to engine extensions
**User-defined functors extend the language**: Native functors add expressiveness but add an unchecked foreign boundary
**Datalog is not a general-purpose runtime**: The assumption of a rule engine and a fixed-point workload is a scope decision
verdict: Datalog's design yields moderate coupling for rule-based querying. The pure rule form separates what is true from how it is derived, and recursion lets a small program express transitive closure and program-analysis queries. Main strengths: a tiny core, powerful recursion, and a strong fit for knowledge-base and program-analysis problems. Main weaknesses: dynamic typing, no module or namespace boundary in the core, no standard package manager, a small ecosystem, slow standardisation, and runtime-only detection of arity and type errors.

energy.text: Runs inside a rule engine or is compiled to another target: energy and time depend heavily on the chosen engine.

ai-readiness.text: Sparse training data and a smaller community: models write Datalog less reliably than SQL.

safety.text: No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

use:data.observation: derive answers from facts and rules

use:query.observation: derive answers from facts and rules

delivery.note: The database engine stores and parses the query text; no compiled unit crosses a boundary.
